content: The six-month BPaLM regimen has demonstrated superior outcomes when compared to the currently recommended regimens lasting nine months or longer. This comparison suggests that the BPaLM regimen should be the preferred treatment option for eligible patient groups. Based on the review and assessments, the new recommendation is to use the BPaLM regimen as the first-line treatment for patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) under routine programmatic conditions. Patients with MDR/RR-TB who are not eligible for this regimen may be treated with one of the nine-month regimens, while longer regimens are reserved for individuals with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones or intolerance to key drugs like bedaquiline, linezolid, or pretomanid. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) focused on direct comparisons within the TB-PRACTECAL trial arms, as randomized trial data were deemed more reliable than indirect or non-randomized comparisons. Although the certainty of evidence from these comparisons was judged to be very low, it was still considered higher than that of indirect comparisons. The BPaLM regimen, as tested in the TB-PRACTECAL trial, showed better treatment success rates, fewer failures or recurrences, and less emerging drug resistance compared to the standard of care (SoC) regimens. The optimal dosing and duration of linezolid within the BPaLM regimen were determined to be 600 mg for 26 weeks. This specific dose and duration were used in subsequent comparisons, leading to conditional recommendations for the BPaLM regimen over longer regimens in patients with MDR/RR-TB and additional fluoroquinolone resistance. The BPaLM regimen was also preferred over the BPaL regimen due to higher treatment success rates and fewer adverse outcomes. Children under 14 years of age were excluded from the TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials, primarily due to the lack of safety data on pretomanid in this age group. As a result, the BPaLM/BPaL regimen is recommended only for adults and adolescents aged 14 years and older. Similarly, pregnant and breastfeeding women were excluded from these trials due to unknown effects of pretomanid on fetal development. Breastfeeding is not recommended for women taking pretomanid, and alternative treatment options should be considered for this subgroup. Patients with extrapulmonary TB, significant liver enzyme abnormalities, cardiac conditions, severe peripheral neuropathy, or very low body mass index (BMI < 17) were also excluded from the trials. These patients may only receive the regimen if the treating physician determines it to be the best option despite these contraindications. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) is critical for the implementation of the BPaLM regimen. Patients with prior use of bedaquiline, pretomanid, or linezolid for more than one month should not be enrolled unless recent DST confirms susceptibility. Fluoroquinolone resistance testing should also be performed before starting treatment. If fluoroquinolone resistance is detected, moxifloxacin should be omitted, and the regimen continued as BPaL. In the absence of resistance, moxifloxacin enhances the regimen's efficacy and provides additional protection against acquired resistance. The WHO recommends strengthening DST services globally to support the implementation of MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens. National and reference laboratories should have the necessary facilities and reagents to perform quality-assured DST. Surveillance of resistance to new medicines should also be incorporated into routine efforts to guide the adoption and use of new regimens. Drug-drug interactions must be carefully managed when co-administering TB and HIV medications. For example, efavirenz significantly reduces pretomanid exposure, so alternative antiretroviral agents should be considered. Dolutegravir-based regimens are preferred for co-administration with the BPaLM/BPaL regimen. Effective patient support is essential to ensure adherence to treatment, monitor for adverse events, and manage drug-drug interactions. Close monitoring for treatment response and emerging drug resistance is also critical to achieving optimal outcomes.
